title: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893
hook: an Upanishad line read out in Chicago: hear, children of immortal bliss

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda in Chicago, greeting a hall of strangers as sisters and brothers, and offering a hymn of many rivers meeting in one sea. Did you greet a room as family? Day nine hundred forty.

Hear, children of immortal bliss. That's an old line from the Upanishads, and some days after his greeting, Vivekananda read it out to the same hall in Chicago. It's an unusual way to address a crowd. Not ladies and gentlemen. Not friends. Not even sisters and brothers this time. Children of immortal bliss: every person in the room, named for what he believed they already were. Today, his longer talk, the one printed as his paper on Hinduism, and the address it turns on.
screen: `HEAR, CHILDREN OF IMMORTAL BLISS.` → `READ OUT IN CHICAGO.` → `WHAT YOU ALREADY ARE.`

segments.voice: The line comes from the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, where a seer calls out to all the children of the immortal, and then says, in effect: I have known the great one, shining like the sun, beyond the darkness, and only by knowing that does anyone pass beyond death. Vivekananda takes that call and turns it toward his listeners. In his paper, he tells them they are not, at bottom, weak or fallen creatures. He calls them children of God, sharers of immortal bliss, and holy. The soul, in the Vedanta he's describing, was never born and never dies; the body and mind change, but what you are underneath does not. Then he makes a second move that matters just as much. Religion, he says, is not finally about accepting a doctrine or agreeing with a creed. It's about realizing: being, and becoming. In the Hindu view he lays out, the whole point is to see the divine directly, not just to hear about it. Images, rituals and scriptures are helps along the road, steps for different people at different places. For the Hindu, he says, a person isn't traveling from error to truth, but from truth to truth, from a lower truth to a higher one. A lower step isn't an error; it's simply where someone stands. So the paper holds two things together. A very high claim about every person in the room, and a very patient view of how people actually get there. Children of immortal bliss, still learning to walk.
screen: `A SEER CALLS OUT TO EVERYONE.` · `NOT WEAK, BUT HOLY.` · `RELIGION IS REALIZING.` · `FROM TRUTH TO TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath come and go. Think of the name you call yourself in your worst moments, the one you'd never say out loud. Notice it, without arguing. Now try the Upanishad's name instead: child of immortal bliss. Say it silently on the out-breath a few times, and notice what part of you resists, and what part leans in. You don't have to believe it to try it on. If you pray, you can rest in a prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Vivekananda. The monk who stood in Chicago and called his listeners children of immortal bliss.
Your line: children of immortal bliss. Today, when you catch yourself using that worst-moment name, swap in the Upanishad's once. Day nine hundred forty.

howItsDone: Vivekananda's paper on Hinduism is read in Vedanta study circles, and the Upanishad's call to the children of immortal bliss is chanted and quoted in Hindu talks and gatherings.

fork.setup: you've got one line to describe every person in a packed hall of strangers. which do you choose?
fork.reveal: Vivekananda borrowed the Upanishad's address, naming his listeners for what he believed they already were.

original.note: Sanskrit, from the Shvetashvatara Upanishad: children of the immortal.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice compliment to an audience.
what it means: in the Vedanta he described, every person is divine at the root, and religion is realizing it.
what a scholar hears: he was reading out the Shvetashvatara Upanishad's call, amritasya putrah, to the hall in Chicago.

sources.ref: Swami Vivekananda, Paper on Hinduism, World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago
sources.work: The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (paraphrased)

notes: All paraphrase. 'Hear, children of immortal bliss' is Vivekananda's English rendering of Shvetashvatara 2.5 (shrinvantu vishve amritasya putrah); it's used in the voice without quotation marks and cited as a paraphrase. Confirm the verse numbers 2.5 and 3.8 for the two lines he joins.

The paper's line that it is a sin to call people sinners is deliberately left out so it can't be heard as aimed at another tradition; the script keeps his positive claim (children of God, sharers of immortal bliss, holy).
Confirm the 'not from error to truth, but from truth to truth' line and the childhood image are in the Paper on Hinduism; both are paraphrased.
'Some days after his greeting' avoids a date; the paper was read on a later day of the Parliament.
Original: अमृतस्य पुत्राः; confirm the plural form as it appears in the verse.
Editor pass: replaced 'Nobody blames a child for being a child' (a childhood image not confirmed in the paper) with a plain restatement of the truth-to-truth line.
